done.why: My fourth death put me in the Void, and the game said nothing more would ever happen to me there. I had drowned my lamp in the lake, so the caves were pitch black, and I gambled on walking through the dark anyway. A grue got me.

about: I'm an adventurer who fell down an endless stair to face a "final test" set by an old, silver-haired man. To prove I'm worthy I have to get through shadowy lands, a duel with a hooded figure and a freezing lake, and every mistake really costs something. He'll bring you back from death a few times, but what you lose stays lost, and after that he gives up on you and goes to look for someone else.

ending.what: The Void ending. After my fourth death the voice said "perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!" and left me suspended in blackness, with the game over for good.

moments.note: "Who do you think you are? Arthur?" when I tried to pull the sword from the rock. Good joke.
The hooded figure turned up and the sword from the junction jumped into my hand, glowing.
I knocked the figure down, but trying to remove its hood just got me stabbed. I couldn't tell what the fight wanted from me.
I died and woke in a prison cell where the old man raised me with his staff. Nice way to handle death.
Getting into the lake made me drop everything, and the lamp shorted out. The warning about the cold was there, but I didn't read it as "you'll lose your light for good".
Diving down to the lakebed and seeing a shiny thing flicker in the sand felt like a real puzzle hint.
I searched the sand and a huge fish swallowed me whole, with no warning at all.
The lamp "will not light again." Right then I knew this run was basically over.
RESTART was refused, in character, and it told me exactly how many lives I had left. Harsh but fair, and it made the last gamble feel tense.
The Void ending was a sad, quiet close. I respected it even though I was annoyed with myself.

wished: Some way to dry out or replace the lamp, or a second light source, after a single mistake.
A clearer sign that going into the lake would cost me the lamp for good, before I did it.
A hint about what beating the hooded figure actually means, since knocking it down and reaching for the hood didn't work.
A chance to grab the shiny object in the sand before the fish ate me.

lines.line: "You have reached the final test, my friend! You are proved clever and powerful, but this is not yet enough! Seek me when you feel yourself worthy!"
lines.why: This gave me my goal straight away: find the old man and prove myself.

lines.line: Who do you think you are? Arthur?
lines.why: Funny, and it told me the sword wasn't going to come out of the rock the obvious way.

lines.line: Slowly and carefully, the figure starts to remove its hood as you fall to the ground, dead.
lines.why: A haunting death line. It made me wonder who was under the hood.

lines.line: It has been in the lake, and it is the worse for it: there is water behind the glass and a smell of wet metal, and it will not light again.
lines.why: The moment I knew my run was doomed. Lovely writing for such a bad turn of events.

lines.line: This world does not start over on request. What you have lost stays lost, and what you have done stays done.
lines.why: It set the stakes clearly and told me I had one life left.

lines.line: "I have waited a long age for you, my friend, but perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!"
lines.why: A sad, final dismissal. It made failing feel like it mattered.

fun.why: The opening, the duel and the lakebed dive were fun. Then losing the lamp shut the run down and left me nothing to do but gamble in the dark.

engagement.why: I had a goal from the first line, and the refusal to restart plus the life count made every choice tense right up to the last step.

difficulty.why: One easy mistake, going into the lake with the lamp, ruined the run for good. The fish death came with no warning, and the duel gave me little feedback about what it wanted.

interestingness.why: The resurrection cell, the limited lives told in the story's own voice, and the ending where the old man gives up on you all made death mean something.

prose.why: The writing was atmospheric throughout. The new lines about blocked passages and the dead lamp were especially good. Some of the fight messages were just standard.
